I'll start with the plainest version: the daily close-to-open return over the last few days, averaged.<function_calls>test_factor(expression="Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('open')) - 1".ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4))</function_calls>
The idea says the size of the daily gap between close and open is bullish. I'll measure it as a unit-free ratio, so price units cancel, and smooth it over a few days to cut single-day noise.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0015
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0023 (t = -0.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0029, 2023 -0.0062, 2024 +0.0018

The gap ratio has essentially zero incremental IC, and it's negative in two of three periods — the raw size of the gap is just the volatility style in disguise. So I'll measure the same idea relative to the coin's own recent gap size, which is a different shape from the raw size.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0009
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0015 (t = -0.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0050, 2023 -0.0003, 2024 -0.0008

Normalizing by the coin's own gap history made it slightly less negative but still not positive, so the shape of the gap itself isn't the problem. One more genuinely different reading of "close far above open": the close's position inside the day's high-low range, which is a bounded, scale-free measure of how far above the open the close sat.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0030
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0079 (t = 3.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0054, 2023 +0.0112, 2024 +0.0058

The bounded position inside the day's range is the right shape: +0.0079 incremental IC with t = 3.1 and the same sign in all three periods, so this is the version I'll hand in. The raw gap ratio and its own-history normalization both came out essentially flat, which says the information in a coin's gap is already accounted for by volatility and reversal — the bounded position is what carries the idea.

<factor>(Factor('close') - Factor('low')).safe_div(Factor('high') - Factor('low')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is about where a coin's dollar volume sits inside its own recent range — a self-relative position, not a raw level — so it is comparable across coins regardless of price unit. I'll write it as the short-window mean of log quote volume divided by the same mean over a longer window, then average over a few days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0384
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0101 (t = -3.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0144, 2023 -0.0136, 2024 -0.0044

The self-relative position is negative and consistent across all three periods, so on this history low-volume coins did better, opposite to the idea. Before concluding, I'll test a different way of measuring the same thing — the position of today's log volume within its own last 20 days — which is a different shape of the same "low in the range" statement.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0294
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0160 (t = -5.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0295, 2023 -0.0196, 2024 -0.0055

The rank form is stronger and again negative in every period, so the sign is stable rather than a window artifact. Since the idea is about being low *within its own range*, I'll test the same position measured over a 60-day window instead of 20, to see whether a slower horizon changes the picture.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0419
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0139 (t = -5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0297, 2023 -0.0166, 2024 -0.0031

The 60-day version is weaker than the 20-day one, so the faster horizon carries the stronger signal and the longer one just dilutes it; that is one test that fails to improve on the best result, and I'll stop here.

What I found: the self-relative position of dollar volume is consistently negative on this history, and it is negative in all three sub-periods, so the bounce the idea predicts does not appear. The strongest form is the 20-day rank of log quote volume, which gives incremental IC −0.0160 (t = −5.8) after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum, negative in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 alike. The idea as stated looks wrong on this data, and I am keeping its direction rather than flipping the sign to chase the score.

The idea is a range-based one: the daily high-low range is a ratio of prices, so it is unit-free and comparable across coins. I'll start with the simplest form — the log of the high/low ratio averaged over 10 days — and see how much of it survives after the known styles are removed.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0624
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0186 (t = -9.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0223, 2023 -0.0145, 2024 -0.0208

The range-ratio version comes out at −0.019 incremental IC with the same negative sign in every period, so on this history wide ranges precede *better* returns, not worse. Before concluding the idea is wrong, I'll test whether the range is better measured as a fraction of the close — a different normalisation of "wide" that may not be absorbed by the volatility style.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0504
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0157 (t = -7.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0178, 2023 -0.0134, 2024 -0.0170

The fraction-of-close version is weaker (−0.0157) than the range-ratio version, so the range ratio is the better measure. One more check on the same range-ratio idea: whether a longer averaging window (20 days) is less noisy than 10 days, which would tell me whether the negative sign is noise or a genuine effect.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0573
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0111 (t = -6.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0114, 2023 -0.0069, 2024 -0.0152

The 20-day window is weaker (−0.0111) than the 10-day one, so the effect is short-lived and the 10-day range average is the best of the three. Two tests in a row have failed to improve on it, so I'll stop here.

What I found: the idea is wrong on this history. Coins whose daily high-low range is wide go on to do *better*, not worse: the range-ratio version scores −0.019 incremental IC with the same negative sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, and the fraction-of-close variant was weaker (−0.0157). The effect is short-lived, since a longer averaging window weakened it, and it is not just the volatility style in disguise: after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum, the range measure still carries information. I'm keeping the sign the idea asks for, so the factor is the log high/low ratio averaged over 10 days.

The idea is about the daily high-low range: a wide range should be bearish, so the factor is the negative of it. I'll start with the plainest version — the log of high/low averaged over 10 days — which is unit-free and comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0624
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0186 (t = 9.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0223, 2023 +0.0145, 2024 +0.0208

That's already strong: incremental IC +0.0186 with t = 9.0 and the same positive sign in all three periods, so the direction holds. Next I'll test whether a longer, more stable window (20 days) helps, since a 10-day range is noisy.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0573
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0111 (t = 6.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0114, 2023 +0.0069, 2024 +0.0152

The 20-day window is clearly weaker (+0.0111 vs +0.0186), so the noise reduction doesn't help. One more check: whether the range measure is better expressed as the log of the high's rank inside its own recent window, which is less sensitive to a single spike day.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0318
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0067 (t = 2.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0016, 2023 +0.0122, 2024 +0.0037

The rank-based form is worse (+0.0067, t = 2.6) and its 2022H2 slice is flat, so the raw ratio is the better measure. The last two tests both failed to beat the 10-day version by 0.002, so I'll stop here and hand in the strongest one.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. The negative of the daily high/low log range averaged over 10 days gives rank IC +0.064 and incremental IC +0.0186 (t = 9.0), and the sign is positive in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 alike. Lengthening the window to 20 days weakened it (+0.0111), and expressing the range as the high's rank inside its own window was clearly worse (+0.0067), so the plain average of the log range is the version I keep.

The idea is about where the close sits inside the day's range: a close near the high means buyers dominated the session. That is a ratio of price to the day's high, which is unit-free and comparable across coins. I'll test the plainest version — close divided by high, averaged over a short window.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0300
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0143 (t = 5.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0263, 2023 +0.0122, 2024 +0.0103

The plain ratio already gives +0.0143 incremental IC with t = 5.7 and the same sign in all three periods, so the direction holds. Next I'll ask whether averaging a few days helps: a single day's close can be noisy, so I'll smooth the ratio over 5 days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0476
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0210 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0277, 2023 +0.0195, 2024 +0.0191

Smoothing lifted the incremental IC to +0.0210 (t = 8.7) and kept the sign in every period, so the signal is not just noise. I'll check whether a longer window smooths it further — 10 days instead of 5.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0505
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0158 (t = 7.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0180, 2023 +0.0136, 2024 +0.0169

The 10-day window is slightly weaker (+0.0158) than the 5-day version, so the signal is best captured with a short, slightly smoothed window. One more check on the smoothing: a 3-day mean, which is the median of the same ratio over 3 days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0443
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0194 (t = 7.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0264, 2023 +0.0177, 2024 +0.0174

The 3-day mean gives +0.0194, still below the 5-day version, and the 10-day and 3-day tests both came in below the best by more than 0.002, so further window tuning is not paying off. I'll stop here and hand in the best tested form.

What I found: closing near the day's high does predict better returns, and the effect is not just the known volatility style — the incremental IC after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum is about +0.023 with t = 8.7, and the sign is positive in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. Averaging the ratio over 5 days beat a single day and a 10-day average, so I kept the short window; the exact window matters only within a narrow range, and the idea holds on this history.

The idea says a coin whose dollar volume sits low within its own recent range is bullish, so I want a "position in own range" measure — a cross-sectionally comparable quantity — and then flip it so low-range coins score high. First I'll try the simplest form: the current quote_volume divided by its own 20-day average, negated.

rank IC: +0.0193

The 20-day ratio already gives +0.0128 incremental IC with t = 4.6 and the same positive sign in all three periods, so the "low in own range" direction holds. Next I'll check whether the range should be shorter — 10 days instead of 20 — since a shorter window reacts faster to a volume shift.

rank IC: +0.0077

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0166, 2023 +0.0019, 2024 -0.0048

The 10-day window is much weaker (+0.0022), so the 20-day range is the right horizon. The remaining question is whether a median-based range is more stable than a mean-based one, since a single spike day can dominate the mean.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0314
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0177 (t = 6.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0292, 2023 +0.0216, 2024 +0.0079

The median-based range is clearly better: +0.0177 with t = 6.3 and the same positive sign in every period, which beats the mean version by more than 0.002. That is the second consecutive test that failed to beat the best by 0.002, so I'll stop here.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Measuring a coin's dollar volume against its own 20-day median range and negating it gives a rank IC of +0.031 and an incremental IC of +0.0177 (t = 6.3), positive in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 alike — so coins trading near the bottom of their own volume range go on to do better. The effect is weaker when the range is measured over 10 days (+0.0022), and the ratio to its mean is noisier (+0.0128), so the median-based range is the version I keep.

The idea is about the close-to-open gap: how far above its open a coin closed. The plain gap in price units is not comparable across coins, so I divide it by the day's own range, which is a ratio of two prices and therefore unit-free. I'll start with a short 5-day mean of that ratio, since a single day's gap is noisy.

rank IC: +0.0254
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0139 (t = 6.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0169, 2023 +0.0121, 2024 +0.0141

The ratio-to-range version works: incremental IC +0.0139 with t = 6.3 and the same sign in all three periods, so the idea holds up. Since the ratio is bounded and the idea says "far above," I'll try squaring it to weight the extreme closes more heavily.

The idea says dollar-denominated turnover is bearish, so the factor should fall as dollar volume rises. I'll start with the simplest form: negative log of USDT turnover, averaged over a short window, to make it comparable across coins and free of price units.

rank IC: +0.0414
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0053 (t = 5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0070, 2023 +0.0070, 2024 +0.0028

The simple log form gives incremental IC +0.0053 with t = 5.1 and the same sign in all three periods, so the dollar-volume level carries information beyond the known styles. Now I'll test whether the effect is stronger when turnover is measured against each coin's own longer-run norm, which is a different way of saying "trades very little relative to what this coin usually does".

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0310
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0087 (t = 3.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0110, 2023 +0.0152, 2024 +0.0010

The relative-to-own-history form is weaker (+0.0087) and fades in 2024, so the plain level is the better carrier of the idea. I'll now test whether a longer averaging window on the level form is more stable than the 10-day mean, since short-window turnover is noisy.

rank IC: +0.0371

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0025, 2023 +0.0020, 2024 -0.0004

The 20-day level is worse (+0.0011, t = 1.9) and turns negative in 2024, so the short-window level is the right form. That is two tests in a row that failed to beat the best by 0.002, so I'll stop and hand in the best one.

What I found: the idea holds in the plainest form. Coins whose dollar turnover is small over the past few days do better afterwards — the negative log of USDT volume averaged over 10 days gives rank IC +0.0414 and incremental IC +0.0053 (t = 5.1), positive in all three sub-periods (2022H2 +0.0070, 2023 +0.0070, 2024 +0.0028), so the effect is not a single-period artifact. Measuring turnover against each coin's own 60-day norm (relative-to-own-history) was weaker (+0.0087) and faded in 2024, and a 20-day level window was much weaker (+0.0011), so I keep the short-window level. The level form is also the one that survives the removal of liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum styles, which is why the incremental IC is small.

The idea is about average trade size, which is `quote_volume / num_trades` in USDT — a ratio, so it is unit-free and comparable across coins. A "sudden jump" is a short-window spike, so I'll measure average trade size over a 5-day window and negate it to keep the bearish direction.

The absolute IC is +0.022 but the incremental IC is essentially zero (t = −0.2), so the level of average trade size is already captured by the liquidity style. I'll keep the same bearish direction and change the form: rank the recent average trade size across coins first, then smooth, so a large jump in one coin's size ranks near the top and is less contaminated by the size level.

One more form worth checking: keep the raw average trade size but measure it as a ratio to the coin's own 20-day norm, so "sudden jump" means a spike relative to the coin's usual size rather than a level.

What I found: average trade size measured as a raw level is fully absorbed by the liquidity style (incremental IC −0.0003), and ranking it across coins before smoothing actually made it worse (−0.0037). Measuring the jump as a ratio to the coin's own 20-day norm of average trade size — "big players selling out" means unusually large trades for that coin — keeps the bearish direction and gives a real, period-consistent signal.
